title: Detecting Phishing in Ethereum Networks using Quantum Machine Learning
authors: Sai Sakunthala Guddanti, Anupama Ray, Mrunal Arun Kumavat, Anil Prabhakar
abstract: This article explores the potential of Quantum Machine Learning (QML), specifically assessing a Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM) and a Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC) for detecting anomalies in real-world financial transaction data. While these QML methods outperform statistical methods, they fall short of cutting-edge deep learning techniques. To bridge this gap, we propose a hybrid quantum-classical ensemble framework that leverages the strengths of both domains. We demonstrate its effectiveness in detecting phishing in Ethereum transaction networks by combining complementary algorithms. The QSVM, whether used individually or in an ensemble, consistently delivered the lowest false negatives and higher recall rates, that are crucial for anomaly detection. To enhance individual models, we encoded the data using novel cascaded Quantum Random Access Coding (QRAC) schemes and compared it with the popular encoding ZZ feature map on both simulators and the IBM Heron quantum processor. For both QSVM and VQC, we consistently observed improvements (13% for QRAC-VQC and 3% for QRAC-QSVM) of QRAC over the ZZ feature map. Notably, certain QML algorithms exhibit remarkable resilience on the IBM Heron quantum processor, approaching simulator-level performance on devices with high quantum volume. This observation underscores the promise of QML despite hardware limitations.
summary: This paper applies Quantum Machine Learning (QML) techniques, specifically QSVM and VQC, to detect phishing attacks on Ethereum transaction networks. The authors introduce a novel cascaded QRAC encoding scheme that improves performance over standard methods. They propose a hybrid quantum-classical ensemble framework, demonstrating its effectiveness while also analyzing the resilience of these models when run on near-term quantum hardware.
main_problem: The primary goal is detecting anomalies, specifically phishing activity, within real-world Ethereum financial transaction networks.
main_result: A hybrid quantum-classical ensemble framework combining QSVM and GCN showed strong performance, with QRAC encoding consistently improving results over standard feature maps on both simulators and hardware.
method: The authors employ Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models like QSVM and VQC, enhanced by novel cascaded Quantum Random Access Coding (QRAC) schemes for data encoding.
model_or_system: The work is tested on quantum computing platforms, including IBM statevector simulators and the physical IBM Heron quantum processor. The core models are QSVM and VQC applied to Ethereum transaction graph data.
key_observables: False negatives count, Recall rates, Macro average of Precision/Recall/F1 score, and performance degradation comparing simulator vs. hardware results.
important_parameters: The dataset is highly imbalanced (2500:1 ratio); encoding schemes include ZZ feature map versus cascaded QRACs; quantum volume is a key hardware metric.
main_assumptions: Performance improvements are demonstrated despite current NISQ hardware limitations, and the authors assume that hybrid classical-quantum approaches can bridge the gap to deep learning techniques.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the geometry of QRAC states on the Bloch sphere (e.g., corners of a square/cube) and detail the feature encoding scheme using orthogonal planes ($	ext{xy, yz, xz}$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the anomaly detection problem to proposing QML models (QSVM/VQC), detailing advanced data encoding techniques (QRAC vs. ZZ map), benchmarking these methods on both simulators and hardware, and finally presenting an ensemble framework for robust results.
why_interesting: While focused on finance, the methodology involves applying quantum feature mapping and kernel estimation to complex, structured data, which shares conceptual links with how entanglement or correlation structures are analyzed in many-body physics simulations.
